rows.title: History of American Indian Nations from Creation through the Present

Analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethnocentrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed in American Indian Studies.

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, ability, tribal citizenship, sovereignty, language, and/or age in Native American communities.

Examine the relationships and impact of Indian individuals, nations, confederacies, and sovereignty prior to and throughout the European imperial and colonial periods by examining and applying skills learned in analyzing original, oral, primary, secondary, and tertiary sources.

Interpret the conflicting role of the U.S. Constitution and legislation to diminish sovereignty while embracing tribal nations’ retention of identity and the impact upon indigenous cultures.
objectives: Draw from and utilize American Indian perspectives, narratives, literature, practices, and histories in a cohesive way from Creation to Contemporary Times.
Identify and apply political concepts and institutions to Indian/early-American relations.

Examine the resilience of tribal identities and peoples with an emphasis on California.

Analyze and compare, through historical documents and narratives, the socio-political relationships of the original Americans and new Americans, including other American Nations and Peoples including Puritans, Quakers, British, Dutch, French, Spanish, Africans, Whites, Latinos, Blacks, Asians, the U.S. and other non-Indian groups with an emphasis on local relations.

Students will explain and assess how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced, enacted, and studied by African Americans are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in migration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies.

Analyze the role played by slave trade in the Atlantic trade, Industrial Revolution, and the development of European capitalism;
Identify the role of African labor in the economies of the English colonies;
Describe the role culture, political institutions, and economic developments played in the emergence of representative government in the English colonies;
Explain the development of colonial laws legalizing slavery and racial oppression;

Explain the role played by African Americans, on both sides of the conflict during the American Revolution, and the impact of Revolutionary ideas on the institution of slavery, on Black self-determination and liberation, and on the African American intelligentsia; at the same time, illustrate that African Americans themselves engendered theory and knowledge that had bearing on ideas of liberation and the development of anti-racism and ideas about racial and social justice;

Examine the philosophical ideas held by the framers on such questions as: the origins and purpose of government, the relationship between individuals and government, and the relationship between government and society;

Identify the emergence of de facto and de jure racial discrimination in the post-revolutionary America and its impact on African Americans;

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, ability, language of age in the history of Africans in America until the Civil War;

Analyze, evaluate, interpret and synthesize primary and secondary materials, and write clear and coherent essays;
